transcript.text: While tracing a separate permissions bug yesterday, I found that 23 legacy admin endpoints update permissions without emitting the invalidation event consumed by the new cache. I have not yet filed the adapter work because I was confirming which endpoints still use that path. The rollout plan must include a binding commitment to build and verify an invalidation adapter for those 23 endpoints before expanding beyond the initial cohort.

transcript.text: Mina, that's a significant finding. The 23 legacy admin endpoints silently bypassing invalidation directly compounds what I saw in the load rehearsal. With a 9-minute p95 propagation lag on the *functioning* invalidation path, any permission changes routed through those uninstrumented endpoints would mean stale authorization data with no invalidation event at all — the cache would serve outdated permissions until the 300-second TTL expires naturally, and potentially longer depending on queue depth. I'd strongly recommend Riley treat both constraints as coupled: the 10% cohort cap and 300-second TTL mitigate the propagation delay I measured, but they don't address the gap Mina identified. The adapter work Mina described should be a hard gate before any expansion beyond the initial cohort, and the initial cohort should be selected to exclude any traffic hitting those legacy endpoints if possible.

transcript.text: Owen's point about coupling the constraints is well taken, and I want to add the customer support perspective on it. The 11 SCIM-managed enterprise accounts I flagged are exactly the kind of accounts where admin permission changes happen frequently through automated provisioning workflows. If any of those accounts were included in the initial cohort and a permission change happened to route through one of the 23 legacy endpoints Mina identified, support would receive tickets about users having stale permissions — and without a playbook explaining the delay, we'd have no way to triage those cases properly. So I agree with excluding those accounts from the first rollout, and I want to confirm that the support playbook I mentioned needs to cover not just the SCIM workflow gap but also how to handle customer reports of delayed permission changes during the rollout period generally. I'll start drafting that playbook as soon as we settle the flag settings.

commitments.detail: Build and verify an invalidation adapter for the 23 legacy admin endpoints before expanding beyond the initial 10% cohort.

Prepare a support playbook covering both SCIM workflow gaps and general customer reports of delayed permission changes during the rollout period before any SCIM-managed enterprise accounts are enabled.
Select the initial 10% cohort to exclude traffic hitting the 23 legacy admin endpoints where possible.
Monitor invalidation-queue propagation and queue depth during the initial cohort rollout to confirm the 9-minute p95 and safe operating limits hold under real traffic.
